column4: Roll Out Equipment Timers Across Boilers, Refrigeration & Kitchen Equipment
column8: An estate-wide programme to fit timers and time-controlled schedules to hot water boilers, refrigeration, and ancillary kitchen equipment (extraction, hand-wash boosters, ancillary heating) so that equipment run-time matches actual trading hours rather than running on a default 24/7 cycle. The same control approach is standardised and rolled out site by site, with savings tracked centrally.
column9:
Hospitality sites run large amounts of equipment on a default 24/7 cycle, regardless of actual trading hours. Hot water boilers, refrigeration, and ancillary kitchen equipment (extraction, ancillary heating, hand-wash boosters) are frequently left running, or running harder than necessary, overnight and outside service hours. None of this generates any customer benefit; all of it costs money and carbon.

Cuts cost — equipment left running overnight or outside service hours generates no customer benefit; on a like-for-like site, overnight waste alone can account for around 30% of an equipment category's total energy spend.
Cuts carbon — directly reduces gas and electricity consumption, with savings that convert cleanly into CO2e for SECR / Scope 1 & 2 reporting.
Low cost, fast payback — typically a capex outlay of a few hundred pounds per site for a payback measured in months, not years.
No impact on guests or food safety — schedules are built around trading hours (with pre-heat buffers) and refrigeration is throttled, never switched off.
Scales predictably — once validated on a pilot, savings per site multiply directly across the estate.
column10:
1.	Audit – meter or estimate actual overnight/out-of-hours energy use per equipment category, per site. Log run hours against trading hours to confirm and quantify the waste.
2.	Pilot – fit a 7-day timer or BMS time-clock to 5–10 representative sites. For boilers, build in a manual boost override for early deliveries or deep cleans, set the schedule to trading hours plus a short pre-heat, and check hot water availability at peak demand.
3.	Standardise – agree one control specification per equipment type — including the validated schedule logic and, for boilers, the override rule — so every site is fitted the same way.
4.	Enforce – lock down manual overrides, or use remote/cloud-managed timers so head office can audit compliance. Review the schedule quarterly, and immediately after any change to opening hours.
5.	Report – track £ and CO2e saved centrally, per site, feeding into both cost reporting and carbon disclosures.
For specific Iteams consider: 
Hot Water Boilers – switch off during confirmed closed, no-demand hours.
Refrigeration – reduce compressor run-time overnight without switching cooling off.
Kitchen Equipment – extraction, ancillary heating and other non-cooling equipment timed to service hours.

column12:
A quick-service restaurant (QSR) in London operated a gas-fired hot water boiler for its kitchen and back-of-house hot water supply. As at many food-service sites, the boiler ran continuously, including through closed overnight hours when no hot water demand existed.
With a daily usage cost of £10 and overnight wastage of 30%, this lead to an annual cost saving of £1095, and a 2.18tCO2e saving/year. Applying the same principle to refrigeration (night blinds to cut compressor run-time) and kitchen ancillary equipment (extraction timed to service hours) at the same site, using industry-benchmark estimates pending on-site validation, adds a further £1,132 and 0.72 tCO2e — taking the combined per-site opportunity to approximately £2,227 and 2.89 tCO2e per year.
